transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (CTO, Sable Systems), Priya Nair (Lead ML Engineer), Jordan Kim (SRE)

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Ava from Redwood, I run accounts for the East region. Diego from our SE team is here to do the product walkthrough and demo. Marcus: thanks for having us.
[00:12] Marcus: Yep thanks Ava. Quick note, we've got a 45 minute block, hope that's ok. Our main goals - want to understand hosted API capabilities for chat generation, streaming latency, and how retries and params work. Also security and data residency requirements.
[00:25] Diego: Great - we'll focus on chat/text generation basics: streaming, params like temperature/top_p/max_tokens, and retry semantics including idempotency keys. I'll share the console and a quick SDK demo.
[00:35] Priya: Sounds good. We have an internal target of 200ms median for short responses (<=100 tokens) and 700ms 95th for longer ones, curious if hosted can hit that.
[00:44] Diego: Noted - we'll show typical numbers and then talk about Dedicated options for tighter SLOs.

Topics:
- Hosted API streaming and how it affects perceived latency
- Request parameters and sampling controls
- Retry behavior, idempotency, and backoff
- Console demo for request inspection and tracing
- Optimize hints (batching, caching, quantization suggestions)
- Security and compliance concerns

[01:10] Diego: Starting the demo - SDK example first. (screen share) Simple chat call: client.chat.create({model: 'redwood-chat-1', messages: [...], stream: true, temperature: 0.2, top_p: 0.9, max_tokens: 256}) - with stream:true we return incremental chunks over SSE or websockets.
[01:35] Marcus: How is stream implemented? We have a lot of small interactive UIs and streaming matters.
[01:40] Diego: We offer server-sent events and websocket streaming. The SDK exposes an async iterator so you can render tokens as they arrive. On the server side we flush partial tokens as soon as the decode emits them; we also support chunked heuristic to avoid tiny packet overhead. That reduces time-to-first-byte significantly.
[01:58] Jordan: Do you support delta updates and role-based fields like function-calls streaming?
[02:05] Diego: Yes, we stream delta chunks including function-calling frames. Function args can arrive incrementally.

[02:20] Priya: For the latency numbers, do you have benchmarks for short responses - e.g., 50 tokens - under hosted?
[02:28] Diego: Hosteds' median for small responses on curated models is usually around 120-220 ms TTFB depending on region and model. For tighter SLOs we recommend Dedicated capacity where you can reserve GPUs and get predictable p95s. We'll send a benchmark sheet.
[02:45] Ava: I'll attach our public performance profile and a sample spreadsheet with measurements.

[03:05] Diego: Moving on to request params - quick overview: temperature controls randomness, top_p for nucleus sampling, max_tokens to cap length, presence/ frequency penalty for repetition. For deterministic outputs set temperature:0 and top_p:1. We also surfaced sampling in the Console so you can tune quickly.
[03:30] Marcus: How do retries work? We have flaky networks and want safe retry semantics so we don't double-charge or get duplicated outputs.
[03:38] Diego: Good question. We recommend idempotency keys for stateful operations. For generate endpoints we have two parts: if you don't get a response due to transient error, our SDK will retry with exponential backoff by default but only for retryable errors (5xx, connection reset). For non-idempotent side-effects you should supply an idempotency key which we respect for a short TTL - the server will dedupe. Also we surface response status codes and detailed error bodies so you can handle them.
[04:05] Priya: Is retry behavior configurable on the client? Rate limiting?
[04:10] Diego: Yes, the SDK (and our HTTP API) exposes retry config. We also expose rate limit headers so you can dynamically backoff. For heavy bursty traffic we recommend token bucket on the client-side and/or request-level throttling.

[04:30] Jordan: For streaming, do retries attempt to resume the stream or restart?
[04:34] Diego: Streams restart; we don't currently resume partial decoder state from the last chunk. For resumable long-running sessions we recommend checkpointing the messages and using the model's context to continue or use KV cache on Dedicated. We're exploring resumable streaming but it's not in the hosted API yet.

[05:00] Ava: Quick Console tour - (screenshare) This is the request inspector, you can replay calls, see token breakdowns, cost estimates per call. You can also toggle streaming to see chunk timings.
[05:20] Marcus: Can we hook tracing into our observability stack?
[05:24] Diego: Yes, we have tracing hooks and you can export logs to your preferred SIEM. We also support trace IDs in request headers for cross-service correlation.

[05:45] Priya: Security: we're SOC 2 and ISO interested, and need SSO/SAML and audit logs, plus KMS for encryption at rest. Also data residency for EU users.
[05:58] Ava: Redwood supports SSO (SAML/Okta), RBAC, audit logs, and integrates with KMS/HSM for private deployments. For hosted we have SOC 2 Type II and can provide the security whitepaper. For strict residency you can pick region or opt for Private (VPC) deployment.
[06:20] Marcus: Do you retain logs or training data? We need guarantees about no persistent retention of customer prompts.
[06:27] Ava: By default we retain logs for troubleshooting with an opt-out for training. We have dataplane options and can set retention windows. We'll share the retention/processing docs.

[06:45] Diego: Back to generation specifics - batching and caching. If you have many concurrent small requests we recommend prefix caching for repeated prompts and intelligent batching on Dedicated. For hosted we have automatic batching but there are tunables in Optimize that suggest batch sizes and quant profiles.
[07:05] Priya: What's Optimize?
[07:08] Diego: It's our cost/perf toolkit - it analyzes traffic patterns and suggests batching/caching, quantization levels, and model variants. It can recommend a lower precision quantized variant if quality stays acceptable. We showed a demo in another call.

[07:25] Marcus: Price sensitivity - how do we trade off cost vs latency?
[07:29] Ava: You can pick cheaper quantized models, increase batching, or run inference on a lower-compute model. Redwood's routing policies can route cold traffic to cheaper variants and latency-sensitive traffic to dedicated low-latency pools. We'll include sample unit economics.

[07:50] Diego: Quick code snippet for retries - show idempotency-key header and how SDK sets exponential backoff. (shares snippet) Also show streaming iterator pattern and SSE vs websocket usage.

[08:20] Priya: About SDK languages - Node, Python, Go?
[08:24] Diego: We have official SDKs for Python and Node, Go SDK in beta, plus a raw HTTP interface. The SDKs handle streaming, retries, and token metrics out of the box.

[08:40] Marcus: We want to run a POC: test 200 concurrent interactive sessions with streaming and measure p95. Are there limits on concurrent streams?
[08:48] Diego: Hosted has soft rate limits; we can increase quota as you ramp. For guaranteed throughput and capacity isolation, Dedicated is recommended. For the POC we can provision a temporary quota bump and run a benchmark from your region.

[09:05] Priya: Any gotchas around tokenization? We use specialized tokenizers for our data.
[09:10] Diego: Tokenization matters for cost estimates - we provide token counters and a tokenization API so you can precompute. Also keep in mind for function-calls and stop sequences. We'll share the tokenizer utility.

(there's some cross-talk and brief audio glitch)

[12:30] Diego: Demoing Console streaming view - you can visually see chunk timing, tokens, and cost. There's also a rerun button which replays the call with same params (useful for repro).

[16:00] Marcus: What about SDK behavior when you change streaming to false - do you get all tokens assembled server-side?
[16:05] Diego: Correct - when stream:false the server buffers and returns the final assembled response; that's sometimes slightly higher TTFB but fewer network packets and simpler client code.

[16:40] Priya: For retries that restart a request, could that double-bill us?
[16:45] Diego: Billing is per successful response; repeated retries that finish will be billed for the tokens generated. However with idempotency keys we avoid duplicate work on our backend for a window. We'll clarify exact billing semantics in the pricing doc.

[18:10] Jordan: Anything for long-lived contexts and KV caches?
[18:15] Diego: We have KV-cache primitives on Dedicated to reuse key-value cached decodings; hosted has prefix caching heuristics. Dedicated gives more direct control and better cache hit rates for chat sessions.

[20:00] Marcus: For compliance, can you provide SOC2 report and pen test summary?
[20:05] Ava: Yes, will attach SOC 2 Type II report and the security whitepaper.

[23:00] Diego: Wrapping up the demo - quick recap: streaming options (SSE/websocket), request params and deterministic settings, retries & idempotency, SDK support and Console tooling, Optimize hints for batching/caching.

[23:30] Marcus: This was helpful. Key blockers are cost and tight latency guarantees - may need Dedicated. Also security docs.

[23:40] Ava: Next steps - we'll send pricing and Dedicated options, security docs, and propose a POC benchmark with a temporary quota bump. Diego will follow up with a benchmark plan.

[24:02] Priya: One more: can Diego's team run an initial test with our sample dataset?
[24:06] Diego: Yes if you send the dataset and SLOs we'll scope it.

[24:20] Ava: Thanks everyone - we'll send notes and a calendar invite for the POC scoping.

[24:30] Marcus: Thanks Ava, Diego.

Action items (recap):
- Ava: pricing, Dedicated options, security docs by 2026-03-06
- Diego: benchmark plan and test harness by 2026-03-08; run initial test once dataset posted
- Priya: share sample dataset and latency targets by 2026-03-06

Closing: call ends ~16:45 UTC.
